source.title: Collaborative Performance Prediction for Large Language Models
source.authors: Qiyuan Zhang; Fuyuan Lyu; Xue Liu; Chen Ma

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream performance prediction using collaborative filtering and downstream benchmark scores, a different method and measure from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study predicts downstream benchmark scores and compares CPP with scaling-law (SL) predictions for scaled models. Results for the general benchmark matrix, factor-importance analyses, and completely new tasks do not directly test V6's prediction for scaled models. Table 4 reports per-model scaled-model results, but its flattened layout does not reliably support assigning all numbers to models and conditions. Results cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study's main object is its own collaborative-filtering predictor. It does, however, report how well a downstream scaling law predicts scaled LLMs' benchmark scores. That law is a sigmoid of normalized score against parameter size, fitted on smaller same-family models. Those scaling-law numbers bear on V6. The CPP numbers do not, because CPP predicts from cross-model similarity rather than from scale.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that collaborative prediction predicts downstream LLM scores well and argue it surpasses traditional scaling laws for scaled LLMs. Their own Figure 5(a) shows a higher MSE for CPP-0 than for SL (0.0280 vs 0.0208); they rest the CPP-0 advantage on task adaptivity. They also argue that factors beyond scaling-law variables matter for downstream prediction.
record.recipe_differences: Uses collaborative filtering over historical model-task scores and optional model/task factors; it does not fit the original pretraining-loss power-law method. It compares against a downstream scaling-law baseline.
record.method_sensitivity: Having prior performance on two tasks changes the comparison: CPP-0 has higher MSE than SL, while CPP-2 has lower MSE. The study also reports separate results for complex reasoning and CoT tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: In Shapley analysis of the factor-enhanced predictor, several non-scale factors carry more weight than parameter size (0.0090). Training data size ranks highest (0.0393), followed by model family (0.0342), batch size (0.0159), context window (0.0111) and FLOPs (0.0109).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Downstream benchmark performance depends on design factors beyond parameters, data and compute, such as model family, batch size and context window.

record.peer_reviewed: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, 2024
record.problems: The main comparison uses reported normalized downstream benchmark scores, not held-out pretraining loss. The authors note that scores from different sources can vary with prompts, model versions, and test sample sizes, while their data collection retains one score per model-task pair. Table 4's flattened presentation prevents reliable extraction of all per-model values here.
record.rows_left_out: Table 4 in Appendix C.2 lists per-model CPP-0/CPP-2 results for scaled LMs, but the flattened text does not reliably map all values to model-condition pairs. Table 1 and Section 5.1 report general matrix-prediction results rather than the scaled-model prediction tested for V6. Table 5 and the new-task discussion evaluate task generalization rather than prediction from model scale.

untested.parts: All of it; no pretraining loss is measured.
All of it; no extrapolation of pretraining loss.
Prediction of downstream performance from pretraining loss. Whether per-task downstream curves are smooth across scale (only aggregate MSE of one constrained sigmoid baseline is reported).
All of it. The SL baseline uses a single fixed coefficient range, and no fitting choices are varied.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V6 labels were built on CPP rows (r1, r3, r5), which measure the study's own method, not scale-based predictability; I relinked those to none. Only the scaling-law baseline rows bear on V6, and that baseline is weak. Its sigmoid coefficients are confined to a range borrowed from Ruan et al., and it is fitted on a few small same-family models, so its poor adaptivity may reflect the baseline setup more than V6 itself. Table 4 and Figure 15 report CPP only, so they need no V6 rows.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of pretraining loss from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its trend with compute.
Effects of depth, width, and other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power laws in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests prediction of downstream benchmark scores for scaled models; does not test whether downstream performance itself follows a particular function of scale or pretraining loss.
Does not test how fitted scaling-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations vary with setup, nor whether pretraining-loss curves bend away from a power law.

rows.subject: Scaled LLMs (aggregate; LLaMA2-70B is given as an example)
rows.operation_detail: Compared CPP-0 downstream score predictions with scaling-law predictions without prior testing information for the model.
rows.measure: MSE loss of predicted versus actual normalized downstream scores
rows.note: The text says CPP predictions were better adapted to task-specific score ranges, while SL achieved a lower MSE and tended to predict around 0.5.
rows.check: This row is the study's own method (CPP-0) compared against the scaling-law baseline. CPP predicts from historical scores of other models, not from scale or loss, so it does not measure V6.

rows.subject: Scaled LLMs (aggregate; LLaMA2-70B is given as an example)
rows.operation_detail: Scaling-law prediction compared with CPP-0 for downstream scores without prior testing information.
rows.measure: MSE loss of predicted versus actual normalized downstream scores
rows.note: Despite lower MSE, the text says SL predictions tended to concentrate around 0.5 and were less adaptive across tasks.
rows.check: The baseline should be actual scores (MSE against truth), not CPP. The SL MSE is 0.0208, but the text says SL predictions 'tend to concentrate around 0.5', so they do not track task-specific ranges. The fit is constrained to w∈[0.5,2], b∈[−10,−3], borrowed from Ruan et al., and uses only 3-5 smaller models per family.

relationships.condition: Sigmoidal downstream scaling law fitted on smaller same-family models (constrained coefficients), predicting larger models' normalized benchmark scores across tasks
relationships.reason: SL MSE is about 0.02, but the predictions cluster near 0.5 and miss task-specific ranges. It is beaten once two of the target model's task scores are known (r2, r4).
relationships.display_finding: Prediction MSE was about 0.02, but estimates clustered near 0.5 and missed task-specific ranges; alternatives performed better once two target-model task scores were available.
